result:
A connection pool keeps a set of already-open database connections alive and lends them out: your code borrows one, runs its queries, and returns it instead of closing it, so the next request reuses the same connection.

It helps because opening a connection is expensive (TCP handshake, TLS, authentication, and on Postgres a whole new server process), often costing more than the query itself, and reuse pays that once instead of per request. The pool also caps the total number of connections, so a traffic spike makes requests queue briefly for a free connection rather than overwhelming the database, which has a hard connection limit and degrades well before reaching it.

The main thing to get right is pool size: too small and requests wait on the pool, too large and you just move the contention into the database. A small pool (roughly a few times the database's core count, shared across all your app instances) usually beats a large one, and you should always return connections promptly, since a leaked or long-held connection starves everyone else.
